speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question of privilege arises from an answer I received from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) on October 31, as it appears at page 805 of Hansard. The question I put regarded a study that was done by the Canadian Dairy Commission on unnatural acids in margarine that are potentially dangerous to people with heart conditions. He responded at that time, as it appears at page 805 of Hansard, by saying:
Personally, I would have no objection whatsoever-
He was referring to the release of the brand names, but he did indicate that he had to check on the legal technicalities. He has not released that list of brand names in spite of the fact that legal interpretations I have from a lawyer for the Canadian Press-and 1 understand the Canadian Dairy Commission feels the same way-would indicate that legally there is no problem in making public the list of brand names of marga-
(Mr. Evans.]
rines which are potentially dangerous to people with heart conditions.
In the House today I also presented a motion asking the government to make that list of brand names public so that people concerned would not have to be afraid that they may be doing something they should not be doing when consuming margarine. When unanimous consent was asked for that motion it was denied.
One newspaper, namely the Kitchener- Waterloo Record, on Saturday was able to obtain a partial list of the brand names concerned and 1 have that partial list before me. In spite of the fact that this partial list is now public, the Minister of Agriculture is still denying freedom of information in respect of the complete list, though he suggested he personally thought the House should be provided with it.
1 feel that my privileges as a member have been violated because I do not have access to that information which the government has and which the minister has said, as reported at page 805 of Hansard, he sees no objection whatsoever to the House having. The lawyers I have checked with told me there are no legal technicalities regarding why we should not have that information. The government has that information and some of it has been leaked to the press, although only a portion of it. The government has still more information, and because of the sloppy way they have handled the issue they are causing needless concern to the Canadian public regarding the types of margarine they are consuming in this country.
If you see that I have a legitimate question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, 1 would ask you to allow me to move a motion which would require the Minister of Agriculture and the Government of Canada to make public the complete list of margarines in this country that are potentially hazardous to people with heart conditions. subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE TAX CREDIT IN RESPECT OF MORTGAGE INTEREST AND PROPERTY TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last night we were treated to the humour of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) and the humourlessness of the hon. member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy). I do not want to take up endless hours of the time of the chamber today but I do hope to focus the attention of the House on some constructive criticisms of this bill. I want to make it clear to the House, being the lead-off speaker for our caucus, that it is not our intention on this bill or any other bill to obstruct, hold up in any way or prevent the government from carrying on with its legislation.
However, there are two things which need to be said. The first is that important differences of principle need to be expressed and discussed both at second reading and in the committee. The second is that the government has the obligation to act in a manner expected of a minority government. If
November 20, 1979

there are constructive proposals coming forward from this caucus on second reading-which there will be and I will be outlining them at the end of my speech-we expect the government to look at them carefully, to consider them and to act as it must, particularly in view of what took place yesterday in Newfoundland and in Saskatchewan. It is a government that needs the support, consensus and agreement of more than its own members.
1 suggest to the Minister of Finance that, while I find his remarks as entertaining as the next person and while I certainly do not mind his bluffs and challenges that we step outside and have a fight like some bar room bully in the back streets of one of our major cities, it would be far better if he were to take seriously the comments, criticisms and remarks which have come forward from this caucus. 1 remind the minister that we have had over a year and a half to consider this legislation and that there has been a considerable amount of discussion about it.
1 am happy that the minister came to his senses with respect to the differences between a deduction and a credit. I recognize that he has taken a small step-a "banana step", as we used to say-toward a reasonable position on the problem. We do not think he has gone far enough. There are still some very severe problems with this legislation and it cannot be passed in its present form.
I am going to outline very carefully, Mr. Speaker, why we want this legislation improved. The first thing we must do is address ourselves to the problem. What is the problem being faced today by many Canadians? I suggest to the government that there are two major problems with respect to housing and poverty in Canada. The first major problem is that there is an affordability crisis in Canadian housing. That is to say, there are far too many households spending far too much of their money on housing. The ironic thing is that the majority of the people who are paying too much money for their houses are not home owners, not mortgage holders, but in fact are renters. Over one million households in Canada are spending more than 30 per cent of their income on housing costs. The vast majority of those people are not home owners, they are tenants. That is the first aspect of the problem the government has to deal with. It is an affordability problem, a crisis related to how much money you have and how much of that money you are spending on housing.
The second problem is the deterioration of the physical standards of housing in many parts of the country but particularly in the inner cities of major urban centres. The inner cities face serious problems in the condition and standards of housing, as do many parts of rural Canada.
So we have two problems. The problem of affordability is tied to how much money you make and is not tied to whether
Mortgage Tax Credit
or not you own a house or pay a mortgage. Then there is the deterioration of the physical standards of housing.
I think we are entitled to ask ourselves what the Liberals did when they were in power. We heard the speech of the hon. member of Winnipeg-Fort Garry who spoke as if he was not one of the brains behind Liberal social policy for the past five years. He spoke as if he were not responsible for AHOP, CHIP, ARP, MURB and all the other features of Liberal genius which we have experienced for five years.

speechtext: He was behind us but he was not one of the brains.

We are entitled to ask ourselves whether Liberal policy was directed to those particular problems. We are also entitled to ask whether this measure put forward by the Minister of Finance deals with those two problems. If it does not deal with them, then I think we are entitled to ask how we can get a better piece of legislation that will deal with them. I do not think that is being obstructionist, ideological, foolish, or is any of the myriad of adjectives the minister has thrown our way this session.
1 might say, Mr. Speaker, that I am always intrigued by the amount of attention the Minister of Finance devotes to this party's caucus. It is getting bigger with every byelection that is held in this country. That may be a sign that we are starting to get to him a little bit.
Let us look at what the Liberals did. Their housing policy can be summarized in one word: retreat. They retreated from CMHC and abandoned it to the provinces. They retreated from their RRAP program by depriving it of funding. We all know that program of assistance for residential property was critical. It would have allowed low income people in the inner cities to improve the physical standards of their housing.

speechtext: Right on.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE TAX CREDIT IN RESPECT OF MORTGAGE INTEREST AND PROPERTY TAX
speechtext:
The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling) agrees with me. He knows how important the RRAP program was in his area. I know how important it was and still is in mine.
I also know, Mr. Speaker, how dishonest the Liberal position was. In their last piece of legislation they promised to make the program universal. It was no longer to be tied to NIP. We had NIP, RRAP, CHIP, AHOP, ARP and MURB. That was Liberal social policy. They made it universal but there was no money behind it. That was typical of the Liberal party in their dying days. They were attempting to satisfy those people who knew that they deserved assistance in upgrading their homes. One the other hand, the Liberals were saying there was no money for the programs they were putting forward. That was the hypocrisy of the Liberal government.

General funding for public housing and co-operative housing was cut back in the final years of the Liberal government. At the present time in the city of Toronto, for instance, no public housing is being constructed, apart from senior citizens' housing. We recognize that senior citizens' housing is very important. On this side of the House we are glad to see that some is still being constructed, but not at the expense of the general level of public housing and not at the expense of the vitality of the co-operative housing sector.
I think Liberal social policy can be described as "nothing for everybody". The policy of the Conservative party is "something for a very special few". It is a Hobson's choice between these two parties, Mr. Speaker-there is either nothing for everybody or something for some people, depending on whether you happen to have a mortgage or own property.
If we can leave for the moment the bankruptcy of Liberal social policy, I think we are entitled to ask the minister what the mortgage tax credit plan does to solve the problem of affordability, which is a concern of renters and home owners, and what does it do for people in inner cities and rural areas who need federal government assistance to fix houses that are deteriorating.
I want to tell the minister about a trip that I took to Washington in company with the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke), Mrs. Pigott, who has moved on to bigger and better things, and two members of the Liberal party. We went there to examine the American taxation scheme with respect to housing. We attended a meeting that 1 will not readily forget with a group of American economists who were advisers to the Congress.
They asked the members of the Conservative party about their proposal so that there could be a free discussion on its merits. First of all, our Conservative colleagues said it was a tax proposal and that it was tax reform designed to give people a tax break. They were asked why they did not bring in a tax credit or tax deduction that would apply to everybody and be universal, and not restrict it only to people who own property. They were asked why they would engage in a policy of hidden expenditures which, we are coming to realize in a more sophisticated understanding of our tax system, is very expensive. It cannot be readily controlled by the government, it creates an additional deficit and it is far more difficult for the government to control when it wants to reduce its deficit. It is a form of hidden spending which is regressive. If it is a tax proposal, why engage in a tax proposal that will give something to people who have property and give nothing to people who do not have property?
Generally speaking, this proposal is going to redistribute income away from poor people and toward people who have more. Well, they hemmed and they hawed and said that it is not only a tax proposal but really an economic proposal. It is really designed to stimulate the economy. One of the economists said that if you want to stimulate the economy, there are much more efficient ways of doing so. There are forms of
[Mr. Rae.)
direct government spending. This is not really a stimulative measure, it is a stimulus that lasts forever. It is not something that you can take away.
The minister knows-he understands something about economic theory, even if he does not always follow it-that there are times when it is important to provide for some stimulus and there are times when it is important to take away. This bill does exactly the reverse. Regardless of what the economic condition of Canada is in 1982, this government will be spending probably more than $2.4 billion on housing subsidies than it is spending today, regardless of whether there will be a downturn, an upturn, a slump or an inflationary cycle at that time. Regardless of what the economic situation is, the minister has committed himself. This completely ties his hand with respect to government economic policy.
Then they said that it was not really economic policy, it was a social policy designed to encourage people to buy their own homes. They replied that if you want to encourage people to buy their own homes for the first time and if you want to focus your attention on new home buyers, why not subsidize interest rates for those first-time home buyers and let them stimulate the new housing market? By doing this you will save a lot of money and accomplish your objective. They finally said that it is really none of those things, it is political. It is politically a very attractive proposal.
To me that was the final revelation of what this proposal is all about. It has nothing to do with taxation because it is an affront to every canon of taxation and tax policy since Adam Smith, and the Minister of Finance knows it. It redistributes income away from lower income people. It is a hidden expenditure. It does nothing for the economy. It is not an effective, efficient, useful or intelligent stimulus for the economy because you cannot take it away once you have given it. As a social policy it stinks because it does not deal with those people who are in most need. Our rate of home ownership is exactly the same as the American rate of home ownership, just hovering over 60 per cent; and we have not had this proposal, they have.
It was a revelation because it told us what the real intentions of the government were. It told us what the objectives were. The objectives were to win an election with an election promise and an election gimmick. Having gone to the people with a gimmick, the government now feel they have to deliver the goods regardless of the cost, the effect, the fairness, the common sense of it, or whether it fits in with the intention of the government to cut down on the deficit. Regardless of any of those things, we have a government that is determined to go ahead.
The Minister of Finance came into this House yesterday and said that if we did not like it we could step outside and have an election.

speechtext:
Let me suggest to the minister that there are a number of amendments which he could consider to deal with the problem. They would allow him to provide the kind of break that he wants to provide and which would also meet some of the criticisms of the opposition, and certainly some of the criticism that has come from this party.
The first is that the credit should not be tied to property. The credit should not be tied to the ownership of property. The credit should be tied to the fact that tenants and homeowners alike are strapped by rising property taxes, rising interest rates and rising rents. If there is room for manoeuvre, I would suggest to the minister that that room is a cost of living tax credit, or, if you like, a shelter tax credit, rather than a tax credit that is tied to mortgage payments and the payment of property tax.
Second, it is said that the credit can be made refundable. I would point out to the minister that hundreds of thousands of citizens, particularly senior citizens, will not get the benefit of this credit because they do not pay any tax. If the minister is determined to carry on with the tax credit the way he seems to be, there is no reason why that tax credit cannot be made refundable even if a person pays no tax. Then a person would get that flat rate regardless of whether he pays tax or not. That would be a message, a message that my friend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has been trying so hard these past days to get out of this government. The message is that yes, this government is prepared to do something for the senior citizens of Canada, that this government is prepared to do something for those people who have no income.
I know the minister very proudly paraded before the House yesterday his statement that, "Well, you want to be quite clear; this does not give anything to people who do not pay tax." I think that is a shame. There are hundreds of thousands of Canadians who do not qualify for this tax credit for the simple and only reason that they do not have any income to declare by April 30, 1980.
I do not think it is beyond the power and imagination of this government, and certainly not beyond the compassion of the hon. member for St. John's West, to think of the people in his
Mortgage Tax Credit
own riding, my riding and ridings throughout this country where there are senior citizens who need a tax break just as much as anybody else. These people can certainly use the cash and deserve it just as much as anybody else. There is no reason why that cannot be accepted by the Conservative government, and the minister knows it.
Another point the Minister of Finance could consider is: why should the tax credit not become greater as one's income becomes lower? Why does the tax credit have to be a bulk sum which is totally unrelated to income? There is no reason, apart from the fact that the Conservative party appears to be determined to distribute money away from those people who are renters towards those people who are not renters, the home owners.
1 am prepared to say today I know that home owners are strapped. I know the home owners in my riding are strapped. There are not too many middle-class trendies in my riding, 1 can tell the minister that right now. There are not too many middle class crazies either. We are determined to see that the government do not benefit home owners at the expense of those people who do not have the political power and clout. Tenants have less influence locally, provincially and nationally over the affairs of this government than the home owners in HUDAC who are a very powerful lobby.
I do not think it is beyond the imagination and capacity of this government to design a tax relief program that goes to people who rent as well as to people who own homes, if that is what the government wants to do. I think the government could do it if it wanted to, if it was not determined for its own private, ideological reasons to see that a particular lobby got a particular boost at a particular time.
I am trying to be as reasonable as I can in making these suggestions to the government. I have given a number of speeches on this subject in the House. We debated it last year when the Liberals were dying. We certainly discussed it during the election and I discussed it during the byelection in Broadview in 1978. Each time I am always struck by the fact that of course there is a problem. What is the problem? The problem is that housing is too expensive and interest rates are too high. Housing is deteriorating in our inner cities and too many people do not make enough money. That means they are paying too much of their money in rent. Those are the four problems. It is not beyond the genius of this government to devise a policy that does not discriminate between tenants and home owners.
I am sorry but I do not accept the view that this mortgage interest tax credit, as the minister says, will cure the common cold, will provide cheap water and give every young person in Canada a chance to buy a house. It is a fraud. It reminds me of the nineteenth century medicine man who came to the frontier and tried to see sell some kind of elixir. We have crazy rates elixir here, snake oil. It is not going to work. It will not cure the common cold.

November 20, 1979
Mortgage Tax Credit
We cannot avoid the fact that if we carry out the policy the government wants to carry out, it will be inflationary and will increase the cost of housing. You are giving people money, but interest rates are already taking it away. We saw that yesterday. 1 saw in this morning's The Globe and Mail that the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Mr. Froese) was saying the same thing. I understand there are others on the Conservative side who feel the same way, and that does not surprise me. They get up in the morning and look in the mirror and know what side their right and their left hand is on. They know what the score is in terms of interest rates. They know the effect. It is only when they come into this House and have to follow a policy line that they find themselves in the position of forgetting which side is up.
The Minister of Finance knows which side is up. He knows what is happening to the housing market. He knows how difficult it is for young people to be able to afford to buy a house. The minister knows that the interest rates we are currently suffering from make it impossible to buy a home. He knows that the effect of a nearly 30 per cent rise in the cost of money since May, 1979, has made it practically impossible for people to buy new homes. He also knows this tax credit does not even go part way toward solving that problem.
I say to the Minister of Finance today that we are prepared to put forward serious and constructive proposals. We are prepared to discuss with him until the cows come home the virtue of bringing in a tax credit program that will stimulate the economy when it needs to be stimulated-and we think it does need to be stimulated. It should be a program that will provide the government with some flexibility, one that will give relief to tenants and home owners alike. However, we are not prepared to support a policy which gives to one group at the expense of another.
Earlier 1 talked of my trip to Washington and the reality that became evident at that time. The reality was that the Conservative party thought they had found manna from heaven. When this idea caught on they thought it was the best thing since sliced bread. However, they are now the government. The Minister of Finance knows that. He has to recognize that not every economist and not every person who has looked at this scheme and has opposed it-and they have opposed it and opposed it-is a bureaucrat, a socialist or an idiot, as he described us yesterday.
The minister knows he cannot dismiss the criticisms of this scheme as some sort of naive attempt at creating political castles in the sky. He knows he cannot get away with that any more. He also knows that some of the criticisms that have been coming forward have been responsible, that some come from people deeply concerned about the fairness of this scheme. They are deeply concerned about the efficiency of it simply from the point of view of effective government spending. The minister knows it comes from people who are concerned about the real effects.
Will it bring down the cost of housing? No, it will not. It will inflate the cost of housing. That is as simple an economic equation as one that tells you if demand goes up, when supply

is constant, when there has been a consistent drag on supply, you know there will be an increase in price. I appeal to the economic common sense of any member of this House to tell me how that cannot be true and how this proposal cannot be inflationary.
It is important for us to realize that the government is somewhat confused. For example, one need only look to the speeches of the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. MacKay), the minister of housing, as the hon. member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry called him. If he had been in the last Parliament, he would know that we do not have a minister of housing. Why not? Because the Liberals got rid of him, with Tory support.

It is true. The ministry of state for housing and urban affairs was abolished by the Liberal party. That is why we had a minister for public works under the old government who was responsible for housing, and why we now have a Minister of Regional Economic Expansion who is responsible for CMHC. It is that neglect of the housing sector from the federal point of view which has created this policy, which is a lousy housing policy, lousy social policy, lousy economic policy and lousy tax policy. However, it can be improved. We are ready to stay here and try to improve it.
I have with me a speech delivered by the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, the minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. He talked of the need for rehabilitation. It was a very sensible speech about the need to preserve and enhance the standard of construction and standard of housing for many people in our inner cities and rural areas. He talked of the importance of rehabilitation. He said, and I quote:
Rehabilitation serves two important social and economic goals: it helps to conserve and recycle scarce resources, and, because it is more labour-intensive than new construction, helps to create more new jobs. To a large extent our efforts will be directed at encouraging the revitalization of inner-city neighbourhoods-building and rebuilding new communities within the existing urban framework.
Where new housing is concerned, I'm sure that the tax credit scheme announced recently by my colleague, the Minister of Finance, John Crosbie, will help substantially in supporting housing demand.
One cannot have it both ways. One cannot talk about spending $2 billion on subsidizing a relatively well-off group of Canadians-not wealthy, but well-off-albeit three million strong. One cannot spend that much money on that group and have very much left over for all that the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion would like to see done.
He says the new housing scheme is going to be directed to new housing. That is rubbish. It directs itself to all housing. It is the most inefficient way of encouraging new housing. If you want to encourage new housing demand, the NDP scheme announced in 1974 and brought to this House since that time, not as a response to the present proposal but as a reiteration of long-standing party policy, simply makes the most sense.
If you want to subsidize interest rates, Mr. Speaker, subsidize interest rates. Do it. If you want to do it, say you are
November 20, 1979

going to do it and tell everybody how much it is costing. Go to the Canadian people and tell them the cost of this program. Do not hide it in tax expenditures the way this proposal is being hidden.
Why should the government pay for all of the subsidy? Why not get the banks, whose profits have been exceedingly high and who have been benefiting from the deferred income debentures which we have been talking about in this House over the past three weeks-they have been benefiting systematically from that-to come into a housing development fund that would be used to subsidize interest rates directly? This is quite apart from the folly of the government's interest rate policy. It is quite apart from the crazy rates we have been suffering from for the past months and years under Liberal and Tory governments. This is a scheme that says that if you want to get interest rates down, do it and tell the people you are doing it. Don't pretend you are selling something, some snake oil that is not really there. Tell them. Be responsible. Live up to the rhetoric which the Minister of Finance has been giving us since he took office.
The difficulty about this government is that it has broken the promises it should have kept and kept the promises it should have broken. If the government was serious about stimulating the economy, it could have brought in a tax cut that applied to all Canadians. There is no reason the two groups singled out by the government in its tax policy since it was elected should have been chosen for special treatment. Who makes up these two groups? First, the doctors, lawyers and accountants who got the benefit of the small business tax credit. The second group consists of the 2.1 million householders who will benefit from this scheme.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have before us Bill C-20 entitled an act to amend the Income Tax Act to provide a tax credit in respect of mortgage interest and home owner property tax. Obviously, some aspects of this bill were to be found for many years in the program of the Social Credit Party of Canada but, Mr. Speaker, I should like to come back immediately to the reasons which have prompted the present government, the Progressive Conservative government, to bring this bill before the House. I shall refer to the words spoken yesterday by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie), as reported on page 1462 of yesterday's Hansard, and I quote the minister:
This plan is to be phased in over four years, as was promised in September of 1978 by the Prime Minister. It was a commitment which aroused a lot of interest during the election campaign. I was one of the principal reasons, 1 believe, that people supported this party-
I think the Minister of Finance and his government are mistaken in their assessment of the situation, because if the Progressive Conservatives were elected on the basis of that promise, how is it then that they were placed third in Quebec in the last general election and managed to have only two
Mortgage Tax Credit
members elected of 75! It is certainly not this measure announced by the government during the campaign which prompted Quebec voters to support the government. And if it is an election promise, then 1 think my colleagues on the government side should be a little more careful when making such assessments. How is it that the government lost both byelections yesterday? It is a much more serious matter, Mr. Speaker, even though the government claims this measure is aimed first of all at relieving home owners. It must be specified that it will relieve some home owners and not all of them, because not all Canadians who own a mortgaged home will be able to benefit from this legislation.
Moreover, the government has stated that it meant also to encourage private ownership. To what extent? Are there any statistical data about this? Were there studies carried out to indicate to hon. members and the Canadian people just how many people this new legislation would encourage to become home owners? My colleagues and I are in doubt about this, Mr. Speaker. I suggest therefore that this second objective should have been looked into more seriously by the government.
And then, it is to give impetus to housing construction. Well, during the last election campaign which ended on May 22 the present government had made all sorts of promises and undertaken not to follow in the steps of the previous government which had always agreed with the decisions of the U.S. Federal Reserve Bank to increase the discount rates-and God knows that the new government has followed these steps, along the same narrow and winding streets of the previous government, not only to adopt but to approve, so to speak and without any qualification, the decisions taken outside our own country in areas which concern us, our country and our fellow Canadians.
To what extent will such legislation stimulate housing construction? I invite the government members and the Minister of Finance to reply to this question. What will be the economic impact of such legislation on the good administration of public affairs and national affairs? Usually, when an incentive program is offered to the population, certain economic consequences are expected, perhaps indirectly, but they still allow the government to increase fiscal and government revenues.
When programs are established to stimulate employment and manpower, a number of Canadians can join the labour market and contribute to increasing public funds through their taxes. However, when restricted economic policies are introduced so that individuals, instead of contributing to public funds, can benefit from social legislation aimed at helping people who would otherwise live in unacceptable circumstances, what are the consequences of this on the budget and the Canadian economy?
Mr. Speaker, 1 listened to and reread the comments made by the three previous speakers: the Minister of Finance, the spokesman for the official opposition and the representative of

November 20, 1979
Mortgage Tax Credit
the New Democratic Party. Not one of them took the trouble to get to the bottomof this issue. The government legislates to reduce arbitrarily the consequences of its action so that legislation is passed whicfr benefits small groups without any guarantee that there will be revenues in return for the state, which means that someone else must pay.
Does this legislation hide anything, since there will be no economic impact to increase public funds? Can we deduce from the start, Mr. Speaker, that we shall have to face increased taxes and direct or indirect income taxes in the next budget tabled in the House by the Minister of Finance? That is the question, that is the problem. They merely act upon the consequences, as the previous government did for 15 years before leaving such a heavy heritage to this government. The present Minister of Finance is in a position to know. In view of the situation he is now experiencing and in view of the previous government's negligence, what is he himself prepared to do so that, as far as the Canadian economy is concerned, we could move toward progress, not toward foreign dependency where others take decisions for us? No, Mr. Speaker, they do not have any solution to put forward.
Yet that measure will cost $575 million to the public treasury in 1979. That measure will cost $1,245 billion in the 1980 budget; that measure will cost $2,015 billion in the 1981 budget. How does the government intend to balance its budget which is already showing a $11.5 billion deficit, and this for three consecutive years, so that the generation of tomorrow will not be left with a heritage of mortgages, debts and taxes which would make practically unthinkable a decent standard of living for them? What do they intend to do to redress the Canadian economy?
Mr. Speaker, the governor of the Bank of Canada himself appeared before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs and stated candidly: Gentlemen, I have practically no room to manoeuvre, the budget deficits of the government are so high, the balance of accounts deficit is so high we have practically no room to manoeuvre. Without any room to manoeuvre, we have a choice between two solutions: either we raise the discount rate, which is going to lead to higher interest rates, or we accept the devaluation of our currency, which is going to place us in a terrible position of dependence on foreigners. This will hurt the Canadian economy and fuel inflation, something which nobody dares assess or predict.
If we have a measure that has no incentive to promote new ownership because the law, even if it is good for a certain category of people, is not part of a more general context, a much broader context, a comprehensive economic policy, a realistic financial and monetary policy taking into account the immense capacity of Canadians, taking into account the enormous resources we have, taking into account both our tremen-

dous energy and scientific potential. If those laws are not part of a more general context, then we are just further increasing public management, government deficits and Canada's dependence on international finance and foreign financial powers.
When you reach the point, Mr. Speaker, where the man who is supposed to be responsible for Canada's monetary policy says to Canadian parliamentarians of all political parties represented in this House of Commons: Listen, I have no other choice but to follow the decisions made abroad. Because those who governed this country-and I am adding this myself because the governor could hardly say so, but you have to add it if you want to have a general overview, if you want to make an objective and realistic assessment of the situation-one just imagines the governor of the Bank of Canada felt like saying: had the government taken its responsibilities, had the country been managed according to sound corporate principles, with balanced budgets, with the kind of programs and policies needed to put Canada on the road to prosperity and development in order that we take up the challenge of the future, we could say this is not legislation for a large number of people but legislation to improve the situation of Canadians and to promote the economy as a whole.
This unfortunately we cannot say because the available information tells us this legislation will benefit only a certain number of home owners while putting pressures on the government deficit and thereby increasing Canada's dependence on foreigners, so that tomorrow, in two or three or five years from now, I wonder what will be left for members to do in this House. We will be rubber stamps, they will tell us. I would like to answer the opposition; unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, I do not have the answer. I cannot answer because we will have to consult with foreign powers, with outside financiers, with the United States, because we do not control our own decisions, we are not masters of our own future. Power has gone into foreign hands. This is the sad part of it. This legislation, which the government themselves boast they got thousand of votes and got elected for, is but a deception act.
By the way, although there are benefits for some home owners, they are preparing sooner or later, tomorrow or next year, to impose new taxes in order to bring back into balance the Canadian economy. Apparently they are at a loss, they have no real solution, nothing of real significance. They show no imagination, they are incapable of showing Canadians from all provinces that there is a future for Canadians, that we have an active government, a resolute government, a government with imagination, a government that is capable of taking up a challenge. They come up with non-measures, under the pretence of having some kind of concern, but this only puts us in a position where we increase our dependence on other countries.
Mr. Speaker, many people will not be eligible for a tax credit under this bill. At the outset of my remarks, I said it was going to "relieve some home owners, not all of them".
November 20, 1979

Moreover, there are all those who pay no income tax. How can someone with a mortgaged home who does not pay any income tax be granted a tax credit? Yet, according to statistics, some 200,000 people have mortgaged homes and pay no income tax. And those who pay no tax are those, need I say, who have comfortable incomes.
Some home owners have already paid off their mortgage because they have worked hard to avoid getting into debt, unlike their governments, and have paid cash so as not to mortgage their future. Those Canadians will not benefit from this measure, and there are millions of them. And what about tenants? Interest rates are included in the rents. What about tenants? These people have to pay their rent. The owner of multiple units pays interest and includes capital costs, interest costs, maintenance costs, etc., in his rents.
Then what will this bill bring indirectly to this group of citizens later on? The budget will then have to be balanced, a hidden tax will have to be collected somewhere. More than half of those five million home owners, Mr. Speaker, will not benefit from it. One has only to refer to the figures given to us by the minister in the House yesterday. Who will benefit most from it? The big owners, those with the largest mortgages, those with the most mortgaged property-it is therefore an incentive to debt-those with the most recent mortgages, those who pay the highest interest rates. The higher the interest rate, the higher the tax credit, within the limits set by the government, of course. Therefore, I say that in the latter case, for those who pay the highest interest rates, it might become a hidden subsidy to financial institutions.
Mr. Speaker, as far as the distribution by province is concerned-because we do have constitutional problems-let us not play the ostrich and bury our heads in the sand. There are regional economic disparities that are extremely important and serious, and which threaten the political structures of our country. Let us look at the number of home owners by province. We see for instance that in Quebec, only 47 per cent of the people own their home, while in Ontario and in the prairies, the percentage of home owners is about 62 per cent. Have compensatory measures been considered in order to counterbalance such inequity? I did not hear a single word from the government-

Montreal Trust reducing mortgage rates.
-because this is news we are not used to-
At last, some good news in the troubled sector of interest rates: Montreal Trust announced yesterday that it was lowering from 14'/2 per cent-

I suggest some recommendations should be made in order to avoid the two dangers 1 just brought to the attention of the House, namely, the indirect incentive to raise interest rates, or rather an indirect intention to prevent the lowering of interest rates. I must say I am somewhat surprised to hear the NDP talk about the banks. Our friends the Creditistes have been doing so for 25 years: I think they are starting to get the message across the way.
I do not know whether the message is better understood because we sit across the way from each other nor if that is the reason why our colleagues of the New Democratic Party are finally looking into that question; because we sit across from them perhaps it helps them to understand better. But, in this connection, all legislation on banks, including the Bank of Canada, should be examined. When, Mr. Speaker, will Canada be able to depend on a Canadian monetary policy? The governor of the Bank of Canada has said that, in fact, there is no Canadian monetary policy. That is our problem.

November 20, 1979

The NDPs are becoming Creditistes. That is our problem. There is no Canadian monetary policy. When are we to have one? In a month, six months, five years or ten years?
Can hon. members on the government side tell us whether we are now in a position to face the challenges of the future with interest rates reaching 14 per cent, 15 per cent, 16 per cent, and perhaps tomorrow, if they ever follow the policy of the Labour party in Great Britain, we will have, as they did there, interest rates of 17 per cent and even 18 per cent, and an inflation rate reaching almost 20 per cent as was the case there at a certain time because there was too much state control, too many public servants, too many bureaucrats and too many restrictions? Are we heading now into that kind of situation? It is about time this government, which is expected to run the affairs of our country, learned the lesson which it was given yesterday when, after only six months in office, it found itself rejected by people in two byelections.
It casts serious doubts on the policies, decisions and attitude of the government. Hon. members on the government side should reflect on this as it means that Canadians who had this opportunity to express their views in two completely different provinces very far from one another have rejected this government, maybe for different reasons, and chosen another political party; but they nevertheless rejected this government. However, there is a common denominator. They chose different political groups for different reasons but they rejected the present government. We should reflect seriously on this. The government ought to respond to the challenge, fulfil not only its electoral promises but also its commitment to govern in the interest of our country and make available to everyone the wealth which is within our reach, Mr. Speaker. To conclude, 1 say that all property taxes should be deductible from income tax. There should be a provision to offset the cost of property taxes paid by tenants so that something be done too for that category of citizens who have been unable to buy a home in their country, in their own province for reasons that would take too much time to explain.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, we are just starting the discussions on this important legislation which gives us the opportunity to discuss an issue that goes far beyond the law itself, dealing as it does with the whole government economic policy. I hope the government will change its mind and that government spokesmen will act positively and announce really effective political, budgetary, legislative and economic measures that will not hide tax increases tomorrow or the day after.

Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to speak on behalf of the government in support of Bill C-20. This being the first occasion I have had the opportunity to speak in the House, I trust I can preface my remarks with some comments about the riding which I have the honour and privilege to represent in this Parliament. In addition, 1 should

like to touch briefly upon the reasons I chose to seek election to Parliament and why I am here in these critical times. I will do so within the context of Bill C-20, a bill which is fundamental to my belief in the importance of encouraging and assisting Canadian families to own homes and thus have a source of personal pride and a personal stake in our nation.
The federal riding of Guelph was created by redistribution prior to the last general election. Much of the riding constitutes the former riding of Wellington, which hon. members opposite will remember was represented by Dr. Frank Maine in the last House. It is a special privilege for me to represent Guelph, as this riding has been noted for its great contributions to the House of Commons. Many members of the House will remember Mr. Alf Hales, who represented Wellington riding for 17 years. He served with distinction, and among many of his accomplishments during his 17 years in Ottawa was the excellent manner in which he served this House as chairman of the Standing Committee on Public Accounts. Mr. Hales is also well known for the key role he played in the development of the parliamentary internship program, a program which has continued with great success and has helped students learn first-hand about this great system of parliamentary government. Recently he was appointed commissioner to study salaries and expenses of senators and members of Parliament.
Guelph was also the home of the Hon. George Drew, the Premier of Ontario from 1943 to 1948. Guelph's contribution of leaders in politics is part of a very long history, as indicated by the fact that Sir Alexander Galt, an original Father of Confederation, was a native son of Guelph and a son of John Galt, the founder of the city.
The rich history of Guelph has literally filled volumes which make enjoyable and rewarding reading for all Canadians interested in this nation's history. Guelph was the home of Colonel John McCrae. He was well known in the first world war and most noted today as the author of the famous poem "In Flanders' Fields".
Guelph has also made important contributions to the field of the arts, most notably led by the world famous opera star, Edward Johnson, in whose memory the Edward Johnson Musical Foundation has sponsored the Guelph spring festival annually.
The city of Guelph, founded in 1827 and which achieved city status over 100 years ago, becoming the ninth City in Ontario, is known to all as the Royal City, named after the Royal Family who eventually changed their name to Windsor.
As you can see, Mr. Speaker, Guelph has enjoyed a history second to none in Canada. More importantly, however, Guelph riding has built upon this rich history to become a prosperous and thriving region today, and the future is bright indeed. A significant part of Guelph's past, present and future strengths is illustrated by the University of Guelph, which began as the Ontario Agricultural College in 1873 and, along with the Ontario Veterinary College, has become world famous for
November 20, 1979

academic excellence. Today the University of Guelph provides an excellent post-secondary education to over 10,000 full-time students, not only from Canada but from throughout the world.
The present riding of Guelph is comprised largely of the four townships of Pilkington, Eramosa, Puslinch and Guelph, in the county of Wellington. The city of Guelph, with a population of 72,000, is the hub of the riding and is surrounded by a number of small and beautiful communities such as Rockwood, Alma, Crieff, and Eden Mills, to mention a few. The rural area is comprised of rich farm land where hardworking farmers have built many prosperous dairy, beef, hog, poultry and cash crop farms which provide an important source of food for the nation and prosperity for the region.
The city of Guelph itself, while maintaining the beauty of its historical past, provides many jobs in business and industry for residents of Guelph and surrounding communities. It is the home of many local Canadian owned companies such as John Rennie Ltd., Hammond Manufacturing and W.C. Wood Company. In addition, some of the world's largest electrical generators are manufactured in Guelph, while at the same time some of the world's smallest and most sophisticated electronic equipment is also manufactured there.
Much of the success that Guelph riding has had in building up such a broad economic base of industry and agriculture is owed to the foresight of the city fathers and various township councils. In years past these councils have fought long and hard to attract business and industry to the city and -

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE TAX CREDIT IN RESPECT OF MORTGAGE INTEREST AND PROPERTY TAX
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker; I will deal directly with the bill.
As you will note, Mr. Speaker, by my accent, I am a Canadian by choice, having come to live in this country after the last war. The visions, the beliefs and the dreams I had when I chose to become a Canadian were well founded. Canada was all I hoped for. We enjoy the political, religious and moral freedoms in Canada that much of the world will never know. It is this desire that caused me to become a member of Parliament.
During the election campaign the Progressive Conservative Party pledged to implement a program of tax credits for home owners' mortgage interest and property taxes, a pledge kept by the introduction of this bill before us today, Bill C-20. The debate on this program during the campaign, and now in the House of Commons, has served to show the differences between the Progressive Conservative Party and the Liberal and New Democratic parties.
With this program, the Progressive Conservative Party, and today through the wisdom of the voters the Progressive Conservative government, have stated in no uncertain terms that we want Canadians to be able to own their own homes. Let me
Mortgage Tax Credit
say to those members opposite that no matter how they tried to disguise their attacks on this program through distortion of fact, it is clear to this House and to the people of Canada that they do not really support the goal of more Canadians being given the opportunity to own a home, and they fail to support the concept of helping the middle class of this country who have borne the brunt of past taxation policies.
The first thing I did when I came to Canada was to buy a small home and invest what little money I had in this country, which brings me to the first point I wish to make about this legislation. The Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) has said that he wants people to have a stake in this country, and that one of the best ways to do this is for Canadians to be able to purchase a home of their own. It is of fundamental importance that individual Canadians have a personal stake in their nation and in their society. This legislation allows existing Canadian home owners and future home owners to deduct their mortgage interest and property taxes from their federal income tax. This will help this goal to be realized.
The ability of Canadians to own a home is of such importance that it must be considered in the broad context of the right to private ownership of property. This right of private ownership of property is fundamental to the basic goals that most Canadians and the members of this House believe in.
First of all, it is belief in pride of ownership to be able to say: 1 have worked for, earned and invested in this, my home. This is the source of great pride and satisfaction for well over 60 per cent of Canadian families. Statistics show that 90 per cent of young Canadians, if they had their way, would own their own homes. This is their major goal. This program will help those who already have homes to be able to keep them in the face of increasing cost of ownership, and it will help many to reach their goal of home ownership who otherwise could not afford to make this investment.
This right to own private property extends beyond pride and personal satisfaction. It is a means of ensuring that Canadian citizens have a personal stake in their country. It is of vital importance to ensure social harmony and social stability, which we cherish so greatly, that we maintain, reinforce and expand the number of Canadians who feel that owning a home is a wonderful means of bringing about this goal.
In conjunction with this is the often overlooked and yet vitally important fact that private ownership of property is a critical means of ensuring that individuals retain their freedom from the state. Just as individuals with a stake in society, such as a home, provide the basis of stability and cohesion in that society, so too do they guard this right against excessive incursions by the state. It provides a strong bulwark against those who would rob us of our freedoms and our rights. Those who have something to lose are those with something to defend.
These broad beliefs and basic tenets of rights and freedoms must be encouraged and supported, and protected from those who would deny them. The hon. members of the NDP are fond of espousing the virtues of Sweden, their idea of a socialist Mecca. Perhaps hon. members will be interested to hear the

November 20, 1979
Mortgage Tax Credit
views of the minister of housing in Sweden when he spoke last June at a United Nations land use seminar. He said that private ownership of property should be eliminated from the dictionaries of the world. I submit that, given their expressed desire to nationalize everything else under the sun, the NDP policy toward home ownership is possibly not too far from that expressed by the minister of housing in Sweden at that United Nations seminar.
I have expressed the reasons I believe it is important to encourage Canadians to own a home-to protect individuals from manipulation by the state, and thereby protect personal freedom and liberty, and to have Canadians own a stake in society with a source of personal pride that provides both social stability and personal incentive.
I would like now to turn my attention to a discussion of how I believe this program of mortgage interest and property tax credits will help enable these goals to be met by helping more Canadians to buy and to afford a home. In so doing, Mr. Speaker, I shall endeavour to provide hon. members opposite with a short lesson on the facts of this policy and the effects it will have, which is something that has been quite alien to their remarks thus far.
Let us examine the opposition criticisms of this program. We in this House know that the only real problem the hon. members opposite have with this program to help Canadians is that their parties did not think of it first. Because of this and for no other reason, they will try to deny Canadians this very important tax relief for home buyers and home owners. Of course, they cannot admit this to the public. They cannot admit that they are willing to deny Canadians this program simply because they failed to think of it themselves. Rather, they have tried to rationalize their untenable and unjustifiable position through the propagation of nonsense and distortion of the facts.
This government will not be deterred from helping Canadians own a home, and the people of Canada will not be hoodwinked by the political opportunism of the Liberals and the New Democratic Party. Rather than take the responsible and honourable route and endorse this legislation, they attack it and try and delay its passage, to the detriment of millions of Canadians. I can only point out to the hon. members that the people of Canada who are waiting anxiously for this program will know who supported this legislation and who tried to prevent it.
What are these ridiculous criticisms that the opposition have expressed against this tax credit? First, they claim it does nothing for renters. It is their typical crying on this sort of thing which pits Canadians against Canadians, as only they do with such relish and ability. In this case they have tried to pit renters against home owners, although the net result has been only to pit both against the opposition parties.
It is never easy to explain to socialists that wealth must be generated before it can be redistributed, that social welfare programs must be paid for somewhere. We in this party see

the same social inequities existing as do the hon. members of the NDP. We, however, realize that the route to addressing these issues rationally and constructively is through encouraging the development of a sound and healthy economy which will provide jobs and incomes. The key, Mr. Speaker, is that we in this party and in this government want to help people to help themselves, and this fundamental ideal extends to our goals to help Canadians own their own homes.
The argument against this program, that it fails to help renters, is unfounded and irresponsible. The truth of the matter bears this out. There are many points to be made that show that to deny this legislation on the alleged basis that it does not help renters is false. First of all, some members of the opposition have suggested the tax credit is discriminatory against renters. This argument is disproved by the fact that renters already enjoy a similar break in that mortgage interest and property taxes are fully deductible for landlords, which provides a significant tax incentive to keep rents down.
Until now renters have indirectly enjoyed the benefits of a program that home owners have been denied. We believe that home owners, too, deserve this benefit which makes housing more attainable and affordable. In denying this program to home owners, the opposition are saying, in effect, that they are willing to discriminate against home owners by denying them the same benefits as renters. We in this party believe that both groups deserve to enjoy the benefits of more affordable accommodation, and this certainly cannot be viewed as discriminatory-
Secondly, the opposition display their ignorance of the housing market when they say that this program will not help renters. I am not too surprised that the opposition cannot see the benefit to renters of having more Canadians move to homes, as their economic policies generally reflect their total ignorance of the market place. I can only assume that this is a case of selective vision, in this instance of not wanting to recognize the obvious. The fact remains, however, that this program will help tenants by drawing off some of the demand pressure for rental accommodation that forces rents up. There are stresses at the present time in the rental market and the people who will be able to purchase homes under this program will help to alleviate that stress.
A recent survey has indicated that 90 per cent of young Canadians want to own a home. This program will help many of those people realize that dream. I have already stated my beliefs in the desirability of encouraging Canadians to own a home, and through this program many Canadians who now rent will be able to purchase a home.
Beyond this direct assistance to future renters, there is an important ancillary benefit for those who continue to rent, either by choice or because of economic circumstances. By drawing many people away from rental accommodation to home owning, there will be a significant reduction in the demand pressure which is pushing up the rental rates. With the virtual halt in the construction of rental accommodation in many parts of Canada as a direct result of rent controls, the vacancy rate in many major cities is critically low. Thus when
November 20, 1979

rent controls are lifted, as they most certainly will be, there will be adjustments upward, as has been indicated in some areas, and there will be a rise in rental rates given the current demand vis-a-vis the supply of rental accommodation. The significant reduction in demand for rental accommodation that we can expect as a direct result of this tax credit program will have a very positive effect on moderating the rise in rental rates. This is simply a fact of the marketplace.
Taken together, these facts show clearly that this program is not discriminatory toward renters, and in fact has benefits for renters, those who are close to and want to purchase homes, those who continue to be renters and want to purchase homes-and those who will continue to be renters in the future. On the whole, this policy is eminently equitable and beneficial to Canadians who require shelter, and this, Mr. Speaker, I believe, includes all Canadians. It is my opinion that this policy will give tenants a better chance to own a home, and I believe that this is socially important. People will be able to spend their working lives building equity in the home, and it will help them in their retirement years.
An hon. member has mentioned the American situation. He said that the United States was trying to get rid of their policy. In April, 1978, The New York Times and CBS conducted a poll on various aspects of the economy. The results were rather overwhelming since nine out of ten people polled favoured retaining a tax reduction for all interest paid on home mortgages. Of the renters, 87 per cent strongly favoured the continuation of the status quo.
The hon. member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) mentioned yesterday, and I think he also stated this in the Speech from the Throne debate, that many people are paying up to 30 per cent of their income on rents, and he felt this was far too high and that something should be done to help renters. We should realize that for anyone purchasing a home today, the gross debt service ratio for home purchasing is 30 per cent of gross income, which covers. principal, interest and taxes. However, when a tenant spends 30 per cent of his income on rent, it includes taxes, heat, hydro, snow removal, repairs, maintenance, and all the other things which a home owner must pay for. The home owner, in addition to the 30 per cent, must pay for the upkeep of utilities in addition to the principal, interest and taxes. Thus the comparisons are simply not valid.
If the hon. member needs further evidence of the need to help home owners with their large obligations, assuming desirability of home ownership for Canadians is not a convincing argument, perhaps some plain statistics will help him out. Over the ten-year period 1968-1978, the average cost of rental accommodation went up 45 per cent, compared to a 95 per cent increase in the consumer price index for that period.
Let us compare this to the costs faced by the home owner. Mortgage interest is up 138 per cent over the same period and owner repairs are up 133 per cent. New homes are up 138 per cent and home owners' insurance is up 355 per cent, while fuel and utilities are up 154 per cent. The simple truth of the matter is that the average working Canadian family has borne the brunt of inflation in the cost of maintaining a roof over
Mortgage Tax Credit
their heads. While the renter has faced over-all increases less than half the average increase in the cost of living, home owners have been faced with increases over-all that are 50 per cent higher than the average cost of living, and three times the impact faced by renters in the same period.
It is a well known fact of the marketplace that rental increases are historically behind the market. The present rent controls, however, are one reason why new rental units are not coming on to the market. The cost of operating an apartment building used to be from 36 per cent to 40 per cent, but today it is 50 per cent to 55 per cent, depending on the type of building. The net income derived from apartment buildings is low. They are uneconomical and therefore will not be built.
Inflationary costs of home ownership have threatened home ownership, Mr. Speaker. For many people the cost of buying and trying to maintain a home has made the prospect only a distant hope when it was basically a goal only a few years ago. This government and this party believe that these Canadians who have worked hard and saved in order to buy their own home should not have their dreams destroyed but, rather, they should be realized.
For many average, middle income Canadians who already have purchased homes, the costs are becoming a burden, forcing many to face the grim prospect of losing their homes. This, Mr. Speaker, is totally unacceptable, and I would urge hon. members opposite to consider these facts when they vote on this legislation. We want to encourage home ownership, not restrict access to it or make it inordinately expensive.
Mr. Speaker, above all, we must not lose sight of who the home owners in Canada are, and who will be the main recipients of the benefits of this tax credit program. Some hon. members opposite have painted a picture of home owners being the wealthy minority of Canadians, but we know full well that the vast majority of Canadian home owners are working class and middle income Canadians. These are the people who pay the vast bulk of the tax load in Canada, and now when their personal stake in society is being threatened the opposition would ignore them.
It is no cliche that it is these Canadians that provide the real backbone of our society. There are tax incentives available to big corporations that fill volumes, social programs that employ hundreds of thousands of dollars and there are subsidies paid for rental housing, yet here we are in the House of Commons trying to pass a tax credit to encourage and assist average, individual Canadians to purchase and own a home, and the opposition is fighting it.
Why, then, does the opposition deny this program for those Canadians who pay the bulk of the tax bill for everything else? Who is going to benefit from this bill? Who is it that the Liberal and new Democratic Party members are denying a modest tax credit? Mr. Speaker, 75 per cent of the homes owned in Canada are owned by families with a total family income of less than $25,000. Over 75 per cent of Canadian families of three or more members, that is, families with

November 20, 1979
Mortgage Tax Credit
children under sixteen, own homes. Given the immense increase in housing costs I alluded to before which are facing home owners, and given the expense involved in raising children, surely hon. members opposite will allow this bill swift passage.
Over 75 per cent of the aggregate mortgage debt in Canada is held by families with children. These are the people who are feeling the burden of high housing and housing related costs. Surely it is time that we in this House realized the great contribution made by working class and middle income Canadians. These people deserve to have a break for once. They should be encouraged to own their own homes. To deny this would be a terrible error of judgment, and so 1 implore all hon. members of this House to pass this legislation quickly.

The plan involves substantial regional inequities which were pointed out quite clearly by my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry last night. These are due to the differing patterns of home ownership and mortgage financing which occur across the country. As a result, Canadians in one part of the country who are home owners and who have the same needs as Canadians in another part of the country will receive differing amounts of benefits from this particular plan, resulting in increased home prices. That point has been
November 20, 1979

well documented by everyone who has any intelligence and has analysed this plan.
The clear statement has come forward that, as a result of the introduction of this plan, demand for housing will increase, which will drive up the price of housing because of supply constraints we now face. As a result the plan benefits current owners at the expense of new first-time owners. The benefits will not get down to the people which the government professes it is trying to help. They will not get down to the first-time buyer because part will be taken away by benefits that accrue to existing home owners who sell their homes.
It is quite clear that if there is an increase in the demand for housing, there will be an increase in demand for mortgage credit. An increase in demand for mortgage credit will increase the interest rate, not reduce the interest rate. It is clear to anyone who understands capital market financing that an increase in the demand for mortgage financing will increase the rate on mortgages.
The main benefits of the plan from an equity perspective go to the existing home owners who are, by and large, better off than average Canadians. As a result, I hold that the plan is inequitable as it stands and should not be carried forward by the government on that basis alone.
Second, with regard to efficiency and necessity, Bill C-20 will lead to a substantial misallocation of scarce investment resources which are needed in this country now to get Canada working again, as the government has told us so many times. Housing has to be considered as a non-productive consumption expenditure. It does not produce any new wealth. The government has been telling us how concerned it is with the production of new wealth. Now they are going to put $2.5 billion to $3 billion in a housing program, a non-productive, non-consumption type activity, instead of putting it into productive activity, perhaps to assist small business in finding equity capital in this country.
When the government rightly points out that we have fallen behind other industrialized countries in our productive investment and in our research and development, and then we are asked to divert $2.5 billion to $3 billion a year into an unnecessary program, I cannot believe this falls within the government's notion of priorities.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question is: who is going to pay and how? There are essentially three ways that we will all pay for this particular program. First, we will all pay with increased taxes whether they be direct or indirect taxes. There is a widespread fear right now that the so-called energy self-sufficiency tax which the government will be bringing forward will in fact be used to divert current budget expenditures on energy conservation programs and release these funds for the payment of the mortgage interest and property tax credit plan.
Second, we will pay through the reduction of other federal programs. We have already seen an indication of that with the reduction plans that the government has for the family allowance and the child deduction. These will be the areas where we will have reductions in programs. These are the ways in which we will pay for this mortgage interest and property tax credit plan.
Finally, when there is not enough money from the tax revenue for this government to bring forward, it will charge us through the route of inflation. Deficit financing will generate additional inflation. This is all from a government committed to the fight against inflation, committed to the restraint of government spending. It is a sham, Mr. Speaker.

Let no one be misled, this is not a free gift from the government. The people of Canada will pay the price. But in any of the above ways, those who are less well off will be forced to pay for the benefits being given to those who are relatively better off. Like my colleague, the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae), I am not saying that Canadians home owners are well off; I am saying that Canadian home owners are on the average better off than individuals who are not home owners.
The distribution of the impact of this particular piece of legislation is certain to be regressive; there can be no doubt about that. My colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry, said last night that only 32 per cent of the households in Canada would benefit. I think what he failed to point out and what it is important to point out is that while 32 per cent of the households in Canada will benefit from the program, 100 per cent of the households will pay for it.
